title: Universal Camera Corp. v. NLRB (1951)
summary: Substantial-evidence review must consider the whole record, including evidence against the agency and the hearing examiner’s contrary findings.
notes: Frankfurter's familiar formulation: 'The substantiality of evidence must take into account whatever in the record fairly detracts from its weight.'

sections.Parties: Universal Camera challenged an NLRB order concerning the discharge of a supervisory employee who had testified at a Board representation hearing. The Board treated the dismissal as an unfair labor practice.
sections.Material Facts: The employer said it dismissed the supervisor for refusing to discipline another employee. The supervisor pointed to the delay after the alleged insubordination and an officer’s earlier accusation that he had committed perjury before the Board. The hearing examiner credited the employer, but the Board reached the opposite conclusion.
sections.Procedural History: The court of appeals enforced the Board’s order and treated the rejected examiner findings as unavailable for its assessment. The Supreme Court vacated and remanded so the appellate court could reassess the whole record with appropriate consideration of the examiner’s findings. The assigned note reports that the Second Circuit later refused enforcement.
sections.Issue: How did the APA and Taft-Hartley Act affect substantial-evidence review, and what weight should the reviewing court give a hearing examiner’s findings rejected by the agency?
sections.Holding: The court must consider the entire record, including evidence that detracts from the agency’s conclusion and the examiner’s report. The examiner’s findings do not bind the Board as a trial finding might bind an appellate court, but they cannot be excluded from review.
sections.Reasoning: The statutes’ history expressed dissatisfaction with review that located isolated supporting evidence and ignored the contrary record. Substantiality therefore depends on the record as a whole. At the same time, courts must respect expertise and may not replace the agency’s choice between two fairly conflicting views simply because they would decide differently. An examiner who heard the witnesses may make supporting evidence less persuasive when the examiner reached a different conclusion, especially where credibility matters. The standard itself remains the same; the evidentiary context changes its application. The Supreme Court did not hold that the employer necessarily had to win and expressly left the appellate court free to grant or deny enforcement on reconsideration. Black and Douglas agreed with Parts I and II but would have accepted the lower court’s approach to the examiner report in Part III.
